publication.title: Grade 4 Social Studies
publication.description: Explore your county, communities, resources and responsible citizenship.

chapters.title: Finding our way
learning_outcomes: Name and label the four compass directions.
Use a map to give clear directions.
Explain why directions are useful.

blocks.content: What you will learn

Name and label the four compass directions.
Use a map to give clear directions.
Explain why directions are useful.

At the school gate, Travis tells a new learner, “The library is that way.” He points towards a building. The learner walks in the wrong direction. Travis realises that pointing is not always enough. A map and clear directions can help people find their way.
The four main directions

A compass helps us find directions. Its four main directions are called cardinal points: north (N), east (E), south (S) and west (W). North and south are opposite each other. East and west are also opposite each other. A compass needle settles approximately along the north–south direction. Its marked end helps us identify north.
On many maps, north is at the top. However, a map may be turned in a different direction. Always look at its north arrow before deciding which way to go.
Look at this simple school map. Read it with north at the top.
School map (north is at the top)

North: School garden | | 
West: Library | Classroom | East: Water tank
 | South: Main gate |
From the classroom, the garden is north, the tank east, the gate south and the library west. The map is schematic, not to scale.

The library is west of the classroom. The water tank is east of the classroom. If David stands at the gate and walks towards the classroom, he moves north. To return to the gate he moves south. A direction describes the position of one place in relation to another place.
Giving clear directions

Suppose a visitor is standing at the library and wants to go to the water tank. First, the visitor moves east to the classroom. The visitor then continues east to the water tank. If the visitor is at the garden and wants to reach the gate, the visitor moves south past the classroom.
When we give directions, we name the starting place, the direction and the destination. We can also mention a landmark along the way. A landmark is a feature that helps people recognise a place.

Directions are useful to people delivering goods, visitors, farmers moving around their land and travellers reading maps. At unfamiliar places, follow safe paths and ask a trusted adult for help. A compass direction does not tell us whether a path is safe.
Try it

Draw a four-point compass rose in your exercise book. Label the directions. Draw a simple plan of your room or school compound with a north arrow. Ask a partner to give directions between two features. If learning at home, write directions between two objects in your drawing.
Check your understanding
1. Name the four cardinal points and their abbreviations.
2. In the school map, which direction is the garden from the classroom?
3. Which direction is the classroom from the water tank?
4. Give directions from the gate to the library.
5. Explain one way directions help people in everyday life.

chapters.title: Knowing our county
learning_outcomes: Find sub-counties on a map of your county.
Identify neighbouring counties.
Compare county sizes using the same scale.
Explain why knowing your county's location and size matters.

blocks.content: What you will learn

Find sub-counties on a map of your county.
Identify neighbouring counties.
Compare county sizes using the same scale.
Explain why knowing your county's location and size matters.

Kenya is divided into 47 counties. A county is an area with its own county government. Counties contain smaller administrative areas called sub-counties. Learning the names of places in our county helps us describe where we live and understand how people obtain services.
Where is our county?

A county map shows its boundaries and important places. A boundary is a line separating one area from another. Two counties are neighbours when they share a boundary. A map key explains the symbols used on a map.

For example, Nairobi County shares boundaries with Kiambu, Kajiado and Machakos counties. Find Nairobi on a county map of Kenya. Then trace its boundary and identify the counties touching it. A county that is close but does not share the boundary is not a neighbouring county in this sense.

A good map of your own county can help you identify sub-counties. Use a current map from a reliable source and ask your teacher or guardian to help you check unfamiliar names. Do not guess a sub-county simply because you have heard the name of a town.
Comparing county sizes

Some counties cover a larger area of land than others. Area tells us how much surface a place occupies. A county with a large area may have fewer residents than a smaller county. Area and population are different measurements.

Compare county outlines drawn at the same scale. Imagine placing equal-sized squares over each outline. An outline that covers more squares has a greater area. Count full squares and estimate the partly covered squares. This gives an approximate comparison, not the exact area.
A large drawing of a small county does not make the real county larger. Check that maps use the same scale before comparing them.
Knowing the location and size of counties helps people plan journeys, locate services and understand their surroundings.
Investigate

With a teacher or trusted adult, use a current county map. Write your county's name, list its sub-counties, and identify its neighbours. Draw an outline, add a north arrow and label neighbouring counties. Compare it with one neighbouring county using the same map scale.
Check your understanding
1. What is a county boundary?
2. Name two counties that share a boundary with Nairobi.
3. What is the difference between a county's area and its population?
4. Why must two maps have the same scale before you compare the sizes of counties?
5. Make a small county fact card with its name, two sub-counties and one neighbour. Check your information against a reliable map.

chapters.title: Land and water features
learning_outcomes: Recognise common land and water features.
Explain how local physical features support life and work.
Make a labelled landscape drawing or model.
Suggest ways to care for physical features.

blocks.content: What you will learn

Recognise common land and water features.
Explain how local physical features support life and work.
Make a labelled landscape drawing or model.
Suggest ways to care for physical features.

When Venessa travels from her home to visit relatives, she notices flat land, raised land and a river running through a valley. These are physical features: natural shapes or features of the Earth's surface. A road, bridge or house is made by people and is not a natural physical feature.
Recognising physical features

A hill is raised land, usually lower than a mountain. A mountain rises high above the surrounding land. A valley is a low area between hills or other raised land. A plain is a broad area of fairly flat land. A plateau is an area of high land with a relatively flat top.
A river is flowing water in a natural channel. A lake is a body of water surrounded by land. Physical features vary from county to county; not every county has a lake, a mountain or a large river.
Reading land shapes

Feature | Shape
Mountain | High raised land
Hill | Lower raised land
Valley | Low land between raised areas
Plateau | High land with a fairly flat top
Plain | Broad, fairly flat land
Compare the shapes. A valley is the low area between raised features. A labelled landscape model can show how these shapes fit together.
A sketch can show the general shape of a feature. It does not have to be a perfect picture of the real landscape. The low area between raised features is a valley.
Why these features matter

Rivers may provide water for farming and other needs when the water is managed safely. Lakes can support fishing, tourism and habitats for living things. Fertile plains and some valleys support farming and settlement. Hills and mountains may attract visitors and contain forests that protect water catchment areas.
Physical features also influence where roads and buildings can be constructed. Building on very steep slopes can be difficult. Settling in areas that often flood can be dangerous.

We care for our physical environment by avoiding littering, protecting vegetation and keeping water sources clean. Do not enter rivers, climb steep slopes or visit unfamiliar places without appropriate adult supervision.
Make a landscape model

Use paper, clay or clean recycled materials to represent a plain, hill, valley and river. Label each feature. Explain how the river may be useful and how people can care for it. Alternatively, draw and label a landscape.
Check your understanding
1. Which feature is a low area between raised land?
2. How is a plateau different from a plain?
3. Give two ways a river can help a community.
4. Draw and label a hill, a valley and a river.
5. Describe one action you can take to protect a physical feature.

chapters.title: Weather and seasons
learning_outcomes: Recognise hot, cold, dry and rainy periods.
Explain how weather influences daily activities.
Choose safe actions during rainy weather.
Record weather in a chart.
Reflect on ways people adapt to seasonal conditions.

blocks.content: What you will learn

Recognise hot, cold, dry and rainy periods.
Explain how weather influences daily activities.
Choose safe actions during rainy weather.
Record weather in a chart.
Reflect on ways people adapt to seasonal conditions.

On a rainy morning, Laban wears a raincoat and leaves home with his guardian earlier than usual. The road is muddy and vehicles move more slowly. On a hot afternoon, he carries drinking water and takes breaks in the shade. Weather affects what people do.
Four common seasonal conditions

In Kenya, we commonly describe periods of weather as hot, cold, dry or rainy. Their timing and duration differ between counties. Hot weather can occur during a dry period, and a rainy period can also be cool. These descriptions are not four fixed, identical seasons across the country.

During hot periods, people may wear light clothing, seek shade and drink safe water regularly. In cold periods, people wear warmer clothes and may change their outdoor activities. During dry periods, water may become scarce, so people conserve water and farmers may adjust their work. Rainy periods can support planting and growth of crops but can also cause mud, floods and delays.
Staying safe on rainy roads

Rain can make road surfaces slippery and reduce drivers' ability to see clearly. Floodwater may conceal holes or strong currents. Pedestrians should use safe crossing places, avoid walking through floodwater and follow a trusted adult's guidance. Never attempt to cross a flooded road, even if another person has crossed it.
Keeping a weather chart
A weather chart records observations in an organised way. Here is an example for five days. These observations are imaginary.

Day | Weather observed | Activity
Monday | Sunny and hot | Rested in shade
Tuesday | Cloudy and cool | Wore a sweater
Wednesday | Rainy | Used a raincoat
Thursday | Rainy | Observed muddy paths safely
Friday | Dry and sunny | Watered plants carefully
One week of observations tells us about that week's weather. It does not prove the beginning or end of a whole season. Keep records over longer periods to notice patterns.
Observe and record

Make a weather chart for seven days. Observe from a safe place at roughly the same time each day. Record what you see, and write how the weather influenced one activity. Compare your results with a friend's.
Check your understanding
1. Name four seasonal conditions people experience in Kenya.
2. Explain one way a dry period affects farming.
3. Why can rainy weather make travel more dangerous?
4. What should a learner do when a usual walking route is flooded?
5. Make a three-day weather chart and explain one pattern you observe.

chapters.title: Keeping our history alive
learning_outcomes: Recognise museums, monuments and cultural centres.
Explain why historic places matter.
Plan or take part in a safe conservation activity.
Explain why heritage deserves care.

blocks.content: What you will learn

Recognise museums, monuments and cultural centres.
Explain why historic places matter.
Plan or take part in a safe conservation activity.
Explain why heritage deserves care.

Rita visits a cultural centre with her family. She sees old tools, musical instruments and photographs. A guide explains how people used them. Rita learns that history is not only something written in a book; people can learn from places, objects and stories.
Historic places and buildings

A museum collects, cares for and displays objects of cultural, historical or scientific importance. A monument is built or preserved to remember a person, event or important part of history. A cultural centre helps communities preserve and share cultural practices, art and knowledge.

Fort Jesus in Mombasa is an example of a historic building. The Nairobi National Museum is an example of a museum. Your county may have historic buildings, monuments, museums or cultural centres of its own. Some places are important to a community even when they are not famous throughout Kenya.
Why should we preserve them?

Historic places help us learn about people's lives in the past. They protect evidence such as objects, photographs, buildings and written records. They can support tourism and provide work for guides and other community members. They may also give people a sense of belonging and respect for different histories.

Old objects and buildings can be damaged by water, careless handling, fire or graffiti. Visitors should obey rules, avoid touching fragile objects without permission and leave displays where they belong. Never collect artefacts from a historic site or remove part of a building as a souvenir.
Our history project

Ask a trusted adult about a historic place in your county. Make a picture booklet with its name, location, what makes it important and one way to protect it. Draw the place if you cannot visit it. If a supervised class visit is possible, take photographs only where permission is given. A supervised litter-collection activity in a safe approved area can help care for a site; do not touch sharp or unknown objects.
Check your understanding
1. What is the purpose of a museum?
2. How is a monument different from a cultural centre?
3. Give two reasons historic places are important.
4. Explain why visitors should not write on an old building.
5. Suggest one safe activity that could help conserve a historic place.
Chapter review

A new learner visits your county. Make a one-page guide with a compass rose, a sketch of a physical feature, a short explanation of suitable clothing for the day's weather, and a suggestion for caring for a local historic place. Use verified local information, not invented facts.

chapters.title: We need one another
learning_outcomes: Identify how people depend on one another.
Explain the benefits of cooperation.
Draw a chart showing interdependence.
Describe a respectful way to support someone.

blocks.content: What you will learn

Identify how people depend on one another.
Explain the benefits of cooperation.
Draw a chart showing interdependence.
Describe a respectful way to support someone.

It is early morning at a market. David's family brings vegetables from their farm. A shopkeeper sells bread, and a transport worker brings sacks of maize to the market. Later, a nurse attends to a patient at the health centre. Each person provides something that other people need. None of them can provide everything alone.
How people depend on one another

Interdependence means that people rely on one another to meet their needs. A farmer grows food, but may need tools, seeds, transport and customers. The customers need the farmer's food. A shopkeeper needs suppliers and buyers. In a health centre, nurses, doctors, cleaners and other workers perform different duties so that patients can receive care.

People also depend on one another in places of worship and in their neighbourhoods. They may encourage one another, share information, help someone who is ill or work together on a community activity. People can cooperate even when they have different beliefs, occupations or backgrounds.
Consider this chain:
From farm to family

Step | Role
1 | Farmer grows beans
2 | Transport worker carries beans
3 | Trader makes beans available
4 | Family buys and cooks beans
Each step contributes to the next. Other relationships, such as unpaid care, may not involve selling a product.

The arrows show how a product reaches a family. Money paid for the beans helps support the people whose work made the beans available. Other relationships, such as helping a neighbour, may not involve money at all.
Why interdependence matters

When people work together, they can accomplish tasks that would be difficult to do alone. They can exchange skills, obtain goods and services, solve problems and support people who need assistance. Cooperation can create friendships and make a community stronger.

For interdependence to benefit everyone, people should treat one another fairly. They should keep promises, respect people's work and avoid taking advantage of others. A person who cannot contribute in the same way as others still deserves respect.

Imagine a water pipe serving several homes is broken. Some neighbours can report the problem, others can help organise a safe temporary supply, and trained workers can repair the pipe. Children should not try to repair the pipe or enter a dangerous work area.
Draw the connections

Choose a product used at home, such as a loaf of bread, a school exercise book or a shirt. Draw a chart showing three or more people involved in making it available. Add a note explaining what each person contributes. With a group, act out the roles; if learning alone, write a short dialogue instead.
Check your understanding
1. What does interdependence mean?
2. Explain how a farmer and a trader depend on each other.
3. Name two people whose work helps a health centre serve patients.
4. Draw a chart showing how a product moves from a producer to a customer.
5. A neighbour is unable to carry a heavy bag. Explain a safe way you could help and why it matters.

chapters.title: Where people live
learning_outcomes: Describe how people are distributed across a county.
Draw simple population patterns.
Explain why understanding population patterns helps communities.

blocks.content: What you will learn

Describe how people are distributed across a county.
Draw simple population patterns.
Explain why understanding population patterns helps communities.

Look out of a vehicle window on a journey from a town to a farming area. You may see many houses close together near a market and fewer houses across a large stretch of farmland. People are not spread evenly across every part of a county.
Patterns of population distribution

Population is the number of people living in a given place. Population distribution describes how those people are spread across that place. When many people live close together, the area is densely populated. When relatively few people live across a large area, it is sparsely populated.

People may live in clusters, with homes grouped together, or along a route such as a road. In some places homes are scattered far apart. A map can show these patterns using dots. In the imaginary maps below, each dot stands for the same number of people.
Three imaginary settlement patterns

Close together | Along a route | Scattered
● ● ● | ● | ●       ●
● ● ● | ● |      ●
● ● ● | ● | ●       ●
The first column shows a cluster, the second a line of people along a route, and the third a dispersed pattern. Each dot represents the same number of people.

A dot map does not usually identify a person's actual house. Its key tells us what each dot represents. A map with more dots in one area shows a greater concentration of the represented population there.
Why distribution varies

People often choose to live near jobs, water, schools, health services and transport routes. Land suitable for farming can attract settlement. Steep slopes, very dry conditions and areas at risk of flooding may make settlement difficult. These are possible influences, not rules that explain every place.

A sparsely populated area may still contain important communities, farms and wildlife habitats. A densely populated area is not automatically a better place to live. Both types of area need appropriate services.
Population maps help people plan schools, roads, health facilities and other services. A county may need different solutions for a village where homes are far apart and a busy urban neighbourhood.
Investigate a pattern

Draw two same-sized rectangles. Put twelve dots close together in one rectangle. Spread twelve dots evenly across the second rectangle. Both rectangles have the same number of dots, but the dots are distributed differently. Explain the difference. With your teacher, compare the exercise with a reliable map of population distribution in your county. Do not mark the location of private homes or identify individual residents.
Check your understanding
1. What is the difference between population and population distribution?
2. What does densely populated mean?
3. Give two possible reasons people may settle near a town.
4. Draw a dot pattern showing homes scattered over a wide area.
5. Why might a county need information about where people live before choosing a location for a new health centre?
Chapter review

Imagine a new market is being built. Draw a simple map showing a road, a cluster of homes and farms with homes spaced far apart. Explain how the market could help the farmers, traders and families depend on one another. Explain which people may need transport to reach the market.

chapters.title: The culture of our county
learning_outcomes: Recognise six aspects of traditional culture.
Illustrate a local cultural practice.
Explain why traditions and cultural diversity matter.

blocks.content: What you will learn

Recognise six aspects of traditional culture.
Illustrate a local cultural practice.
Explain why traditions and cultural diversity matter.

At a cultural day in school, Luca watches a group perform a traditional dance. Other learners display baskets, clothing, musical instruments and drawings of houses. Each group explains something about the people who developed or use those items. No single display tells the whole story of a community.
Ways people express culture

Culture includes the ways people live, the knowledge they share, their beliefs, arts and customs. Traditional culture includes practices and knowledge passed from older generations to younger ones. Culture can also change over time.

People express culture in many ways. Traditional clothing may be worn for ceremonies or everyday activities. Food can reflect crops, animals, cooking methods and local knowledge. Housing may use materials available in an area. A basket, pot, stool or tool made by people is an artefact. Traditional sports and games allow people to enjoy themselves and learn skills. Festivals and ceremonies may mark important occasions or bring communities together.

For example, a woven basket can show knowledge of suitable fibres, patterns and weaving techniques. Different communities may make different kinds of baskets for carrying, storage or decoration. We can appreciate the skill without assuming that everyone in a community uses the same design.
Why culture is important

Culture helps people share knowledge, express their identity and learn about their history. Traditional games, songs and stories can bring generations together. Crafts can support livelihoods. Cultural exchanges allow people to learn from one another.

Kenya has many communities and many cultural traditions. Families may practise a mixture of traditions, adopt new ones or choose not to practise particular customs. Treat every learner's background with respect. A cultural practice is not automatically acceptable just because it is old. Practices that harm people or violate their rights should not be continued.
Our culture gallery

Choose one of these six categories: dress, food, housing, artefacts, sports and games, or festivals and ceremonies. Make a drawing or model, or interview a willing adult about an example. Label your display and explain what it is used for. Respect family privacy and ask permission before recording or photographing anyone.
Check your understanding
1. Name six ways people express traditional culture.
2. What is an artefact? Give an example.
3. Explain two reasons traditional culture is important.
4. Draw one example of traditional housing or clothing and label two features.
5. Explain how you would respond respectfully if a classmate practises a different tradition.

chapters.title: Our school
learning_outcomes: Tell a school's history in time order.
Explain school values.
Recite or explain the school motto.
Describe responsible ways to follow school rules.

blocks.content: What you will learn

Tell a school's history in time order.
Explain school values.
Recite or explain the school motto.
Describe responsible ways to follow school rules.

Joy notices an old photograph in the school office. The classrooms in the photograph look different from those she sees today. Her teacher explains that the school has changed over the years. Like communities, schools have histories, values and rules.
The history of a school

The history of a school is the story of how it began and changed. It may include when the school opened, its first classrooms, important people, changes in enrolment or achievements. To tell a school's history accurately, collect information from reliable sources such as school records, old photographs or a conversation with a member of the school administration.
A timeline places events in the order in which they happened. Here is an imaginary example, not the history of a real school.

Year | Event
2010 | School opened with two classrooms
2015 | A library was built
2022 | A new classroom block opened
If two sources disagree about a date, ask for clarification instead of selecting a date at random.
School values, motto and rules

Values are principles that guide the way people behave. A school may value honesty, responsibility, respect and hard work. Learners demonstrate honesty when they return something they find. They show responsibility by caring for shared materials and completing agreed duties.
A motto is a short statement that expresses an aim or guiding idea. An imaginary school's motto might be “Learn, Serve, Grow.” This is only an example; use the actual wording of your school's motto.

Rules explain what learners and other members of the school community are expected to do. Rules help maintain safety, fairness, order and a good learning environment. Being disciplined means making responsible choices, even when nobody is watching. A learner should seek help from a trusted adult when a rule seems unsafe or unfair.
Make a school story poster

Collect three confirmed events from your school's history. Arrange them in a timeline. Write two values and the school's actual motto. Add one example of how to follow a school rule. If learning independently, use a school you previously attended or a fictional example clearly labelled as such.
Check your understanding
1. Name two sources you could use to learn your school's history.
2. Arrange these imaginary events in time order: new library in 2020; school opened in 2005; new classrooms in 2012.
3. Explain the difference between a school motto and a school rule.
4. Recite your school's motto and explain its meaning, or explain the meaning of the example motto above.
5. Give one way you can demonstrate responsibility at school.
Chapter review
Make a display titled “Our community, our school.” Include one example of cultural knowledge, a brief school timeline and a value that helps people with different backgrounds learn together.

chapters.title: How people earn a living
learning_outcomes: Recognise useful local resources.
Identify economic activities.
Explain their benefits.
Take part in a safe supervised economic learning activity.
Explain why economic work and resource care matter.

blocks.content: What you will learn

Recognise useful local resources.
Identify economic activities.
Explain their benefits.
Take part in a safe supervised economic learning activity.
Explain why economic work and resource care matter.

Max walks through a local market and sees vegetables, baskets, shoes and people offering repair services. Behind each of these goods or services is someone's work. Some people grow or make things; others transport, sell or repair them.
Resources in our county

A resource is something useful that people can use to meet a need. Natural resources include land, water, soil, forests and minerals. People also use their knowledge, skills, tools and machines to carry out work. Different counties have different resources and opportunities.

Economic activities are activities through which people produce, distribute or exchange goods and services to meet needs and earn a living. Farming produces food and other products. Fishing provides fish. Trading makes goods available to buyers. Transport moves people and goods. Tourism involves services for visitors, including guiding and accommodation. Craftwork and manufacturing turn materials into useful products.

A community with suitable soils and reliable water may grow crops. A community near a lake may have fishing activities. A busy town may have shops, workshops and transport services. A county may support many different activities at the same time.
Why economic activities matter

Economic activities provide goods, services, jobs and income. Income helps families buy food, pay for transport and meet other needs. The goods and services produced by one group can help another group carry out its work.

For example, a carpenter uses timber, tools and skills to make a table. A trader supplies the tools, a transport worker carries materials, and a customer buys the table. Each contributes to the activity.

Resources need care. Cutting trees without replacing them can harm forests and water catchment areas. Dumping waste into rivers can damage water resources. People can conserve resources by reducing waste, reusing suitable materials, planting appropriate trees and using water carefully.

Children can learn about economic activities through supervised gardening, craftwork, market simulations or interviews. Learning activities should be safe and age-appropriate; children must not be sent to work in dangerous conditions or miss school to earn money.
Make an economic activity poster

Choose an economic activity practised in your county. Draw the resource or material used, the work people do and the resulting product or service. Explain one benefit and one way the resource can be conserved.
Check your understanding
1. What is a resource? Give two examples of natural resources.
2. Name three economic activities and describe a product or service from each.
3. Explain how trading helps farmers and families.
4. Why should people protect water sources while carrying out economic activities?
5. Describe a safe activity you could take part in with adult guidance.

chapters.title: Industries in our county
learning_outcomes: Identify local industries.
Explain how industries benefit communities.
Locate an industry on a map.
Explain why industries must operate responsibly.

blocks.content: What you will learn

Identify local industries.
Explain how industries benefit communities.
Locate an industry on a map.
Explain why industries must operate responsibly.

Imagine two families buying yoghurt at a shop. Before reaching the shop, milk was collected, processed, packaged and transported. The finished product is the result of work carried out in a series of places.
From raw material to product

An industry is an organised economic activity producing goods or providing services. Manufacturing and processing industries make or change products using materials, equipment and workers' skills. A raw material is an input used to make a product.

Raw material | Example of industry | Product
Milk | Dairy processing | Yoghurt
Timber | Furniture making | Chair
Clay | Brick making | Bricks
Grain | Milling | Flour
A cottage industry is a small-scale industry, sometimes operating in a home or small workshop. A large factory may use more workers, machinery and materials. Both can make useful products.

An industry may be located near raw materials, workers, reliable water, electricity, transport routes or customers. A milk-processing plant may need reliable transport from dairy farms. A furniture workshop may need a supply of timber from lawful and sustainable sources.
Benefits and responsibilities

Industries provide jobs, goods and income. They can add value to raw materials, such as turning grain into flour, and support transport and trading businesses. County governments and communities can benefit from lawful business activity and appropriate services.

Industries must also manage waste, protect workers and reduce pollution. Factory machinery, chemicals, dust and hot surfaces can be dangerous. Children should visit industries only in an approved, supervised group and follow all safety instructions. Never operate equipment during a visit unless an appropriate safe learning activity has been authorised by the responsible adults.
Follow a product
Draw a flow diagram for a familiar product:
Raw material → Processing or making → Finished product → Transport and sale

Identify an actual industry or workshop in your county using a reliable source. Locate it on a map with your teacher. Explain what it makes, one reason for its location and one benefit to the community. If an actual visit is not possible, use an approved photograph, video or interview.
Check your understanding
1. What is a raw material?
2. Name an industry that uses milk and one product it makes.
3. Explain two reasons an industry may be located near a road.
4. Give two benefits industries bring to a county.
5. Draw a flow diagram showing how grain can become flour and reach a customer.

chapters.title: Starting an enterprise project at school
learning_outcomes: Choose a suitable school enterprise.
Plan and take part in a safe supervised project.
Share responsibilities and keep honest records.

blocks.content: What you will learn

Choose a suitable school enterprise.
Plan and take part in a safe supervised project.
Share responsibilities and keep honest records.

Hadassa's class notices that many learners need bookmarks. The class decides to make bookmarks from clean card left over from other activities. They ask their teacher for permission, discuss what is needed and agree how to share the work.
Choosing a useful project

An enterprise project is an organised activity that creates a useful good or service, sometimes for sale. Possible supervised school projects include seedlings, simple crafts, reusable bookmarks or a vegetable garden. A good project is safe, useful, affordable, suitable for the learners and possible with the available resources.
Before choosing, ask: Who needs the product? What materials do we have? How much will the materials cost? Who will do each task? How can we avoid waste and keep everyone safe?
Planning, making and keeping records

The bookmark group plans its project. One team designs the bookmarks, another prepares clean materials, and another checks quality. The teacher supervises the use of scissors and all money handling. Learners who do not want to cut or draw can help with counting, organising or checking.
Here is an imaginary project record.

Item | Amount
Card and string | KSh 80
Markers | KSh 40
Total cost | KSh 120
Money received from sales | KSh 160
Amount remaining after costs | KSh 40

The difference between money received and project costs is KSh 160 − KSh 120 = KSh 40. This is the surplus in the simple example. If the money received is less than the costs, the project has a loss. Keep accurate records even when a project does not make money.
Working together ethically

Ethics are principles of right conduct. In an enterprise, learners show ethics by being honest about costs and sales, treating customers fairly, sharing tasks fairly, caring for materials and reporting problems. No learner should be forced to pay, sell goods or take unsafe tasks.

A group can also make reflective paper designs or models of visibility aids to discuss road safety. A homemade classroom model is not certified protective equipment and must not be relied on in traffic.
Our project plan

With your teacher, choose a safe project and make a plan: purpose, materials, cost estimate, roles, safety rules, record of work and how to judge the outcome. Make or model the product. Review what went well, what could improve and how the group treated its members. If learning alone, prepare a paper plan rather than handling real sales.
Check your understanding
1. Suggest two suitable school enterprise projects.
2. Explain why a group should plan before buying materials.
3. A group spends KSh 90 and receives KSh 120. How much remains after costs?
4. Give two examples of honest behaviour in an enterprise.
5. Create a plan for a small school project and explain how every group member could contribute.
Chapter review

Choose a useful product made or sold in your county. Explain its raw materials, the people involved in producing it, how customers obtain it and how a school group could safely model a small enterprise related to the product.

chapters.title: Being a good citizen at school
learning_outcomes: Identify qualities of good citizenship.
Practise responsible and inclusive actions.
Explain why those qualities matter.

blocks.content: What you will learn

Identify qualities of good citizenship.
Practise responsible and inclusive actions.
Explain why those qualities matter.
One morning, Mike finds a pencil case beside the classroom door. Nobody sees him pick it up. He takes it to his teacher so that its owner can collect it. Mike has made an honest choice.
Qualities of a good citizen

Citizenship involves belonging to a community and taking part responsibly in its life. Good citizenship at school can be seen through actions: telling the truth, respecting others, sharing fairly, following reasonable safety rules, caring for property and helping people who need assistance.

A learner who finds a lost item returns it. A learner who borrows a book returns it in good condition. A learner who disagrees with a classmate listens before responding. These actions show honesty, responsibility and respect.

Good citizens do not have to agree with everyone. They can express different opinions politely and report unsafe or unfair treatment to a trusted adult. They include learners who have different abilities, backgrounds or beliefs.

Citizenship also matters when using digital devices. A responsible digital citizen does not share someone's picture or private information without permission, does not spread unkind messages and asks for help when something online feels unsafe.
Put citizenship into practice

Choose one duty you can carry out safely for a week, such as organising shared books, including others in games or using materials carefully. Record how the action helped the community. At the end of the week, reflect on what you could improve.
Check your understanding
1. Name four qualities of a good citizen at school.
2. Why is returning a lost pencil case an example of honesty?
3. Describe a responsible way to disagree with a classmate.
4. A group refuses to include a learner because of a disability. Suggest a fair action.
5. Give one example of good digital citizenship.

chapters.title: Living peacefully with others
learning_outcomes: Identify ways to promote peace.
Use peaceful responses to ordinary disagreements.
Plan an activity that supports peace and safety.

blocks.content: What you will learn

Identify ways to promote peace.
Use peaceful responses to ordinary disagreements.
Plan an activity that supports peace and safety.

Two learners want to use the same ball during break. They begin arguing about who should play first. A third learner suggests that each group take turns for an agreed period. The learners decide on a fair arrangement and continue playing.
What promotes peace?

Peace is more than the absence of fighting. People live peacefully when they feel safe, respect one another and resolve disagreements without harming others. Fair rules, honest communication, patience, cooperation and respect for differences can help promote peace.

Conflict can arise when people disagree, feel left out or misunderstand each other. Feeling angry is not wrong, but hurting another person is not an acceptable response. A learner can move away from an argument, calm down, explain the problem respectfully and seek help from a trusted adult.

For an ordinary disagreement between learners who feel safe, both may listen to each other, identify the problem, suggest fair solutions and agree on a way forward. Nobody should be pressured to negotiate with someone who is threatening or repeatedly bullying them. Safety comes first.
Building peace at school

A peace corner can provide a quiet supervised place for reflection. A peace poster can remind learners to include others and seek help. A school may organise cooperative games, discussion circles or an approved nature trail where learners practise sharing and working together.

A peacebuilding activity should have a clear purpose. For example, a class could agree to reduce name-calling by practising respectful words, reporting bullying and checking at the end of each week whether everyone feels included.
Plan a peace activity

With your teacher, identify a common, non-private classroom problem. Write two peaceful ways to respond. Design a poster or organise a cooperative activity. Do not use real classmates' names in a poster about disagreements. If you are working alone, write a dialogue showing a peaceful solution.
Check your understanding
1. Name three factors that promote peace at school.
2. How can a learner respond when feeling angry during a disagreement?
3. Explain why taking turns can help resolve a conflict over a shared item.
4. What should you do if another learner threatens your safety?
5. Describe a peacebuilding activity and how you would know whether it helped.

chapters.title: Every child has rights
learning_outcomes: Recognise forms of child abuse and exploitation.
Explain why abuse can occur without blaming children.
Explain possible effects of abuse.
Identify safe ways to seek help and protect children's rights.

blocks.content: What you will learn

Recognise forms of child abuse and exploitation.
Explain why abuse can occur without blaming children.
Explain possible effects of abuse.
Identify safe ways to seek help and protect children's rights.
Children need care, protection and opportunities to grow and learn. Every child deserves respect and safety, regardless of their family, gender, disability or background.
Rights and responsibilities

A right is something a person is entitled to. Children have rights to education, protection from harm, care, dignity and other basic needs. Responsibilities are actions we take to care for ourselves and respect others, such as keeping learning materials safe and treating people kindly. A child's rights do not disappear because the child makes a mistake or fails to carry out a responsibility.

Child abuse means harming a child or failing to protect a child from serious harm. It includes physical, emotional or sexual abuse, exploitation and neglect. Sexual abuse includes inappropriate sexual touching or conduct involving a child. A child is never responsible for being abused.

Some harmful practices include early or forced marriage, female genital mutilation (FGM), slavery, child trafficking and forced labour. FGM involves harming a girl's genital organs for non-medical reasons. These practices violate children's safety and dignity. Children with disabilities may also face mistreatment or exclusion. Everyone has an equal right to protection.

Unsafe or unauthorised school transport can put children at risk. Use transport arranged and approved by responsible adults, wear a seat belt where provided and tell a trusted adult if transport feels unsafe.
Why abuse happens and how it affects children

Abuse can occur when people misuse power, ignore children's rights, exploit children or continue harmful practices. Poverty and lack of knowledge may increase risks, but they never excuse harming a child.

Abuse can cause injury, fear, sadness, interrupted schooling and difficulty trusting others. Different children respond in different ways. Support and protection from caring adults and trained professionals can help.
Seeking protection and promoting rights

If someone hurts you, makes you feel unsafe or asks you to keep an unsafe secret, tell a trusted adult, such as a teacher, caregiver or another safe adult. If the first adult does not help, tell another. You do not have to face the situation alone or investigate it yourself. If you are in immediate danger, move to a safer place if you can and seek adult or emergency assistance.

A class can promote children's rights through a poster about kindness, inclusion, safe transport and seeking help. No learner should be asked to tell a personal story of abuse in front of the class. Adults are responsible for protection and for responding safely to a disclosure.
Check your understanding
1. Give three examples of children's rights.
2. Explain why a child's rights do not depend on whether they finish their duties.
3. Name three forms of child abuse or exploitation and explain why they are harmful.
4. Explain one possible effect of child abuse on a learner's education.
5. What could a child do if a trusted adult does not respond to a safety concern?

chapters.title: Making decisions together
learning_outcomes: Identify democratic practices at school.
Explain why fair participation matters.
Practise a fair decision-making process.
Respect different views and minority rights.

blocks.content: What you will learn

Identify democratic practices at school.
Explain why fair participation matters.
Practise a fair decision-making process.
Respect different views and minority rights.

A class wants to choose a game for a special activity. Learners suggest several suitable games. They discuss the choices, listen to different opinions and vote. The teacher checks that every proposed game is safe and accessible. The class accepts the agreed decision while respecting those who preferred a different game.
Democracy at school

Democracy is a way of making decisions in which people have opportunities to participate and express their views. Democratic practices include fair elections, listening to different opinions, consultation and shared decision-making.

A democratic process should have clear and fair rules. Candidates should have an equal chance to explain their ideas. Eligible voters should be able to choose freely without threats or unfair pressure. Votes should be counted honestly.

For example, a class electing a representative can agree on the role, invite willing candidates, hear their ideas, conduct a fair vote, count votes and announce the result. A secret ballot can help learners make a private choice. The winner should serve the whole class, including learners who voted for someone else.
Democracy helps people participate in decisions, practise responsibility and choose leaders fairly. A majority decision does not permit people to mistreat a minority or ignore safety and rights.
Hold a mock election

With your teacher, choose a fictional class role or harmless classroom decision. Establish fair rules, invite volunteers to explain their ideas, vote and count the results. Discuss how the process could include everyone. If learning independently, design a sample ballot and describe how the votes would be counted.
Check your understanding
1. What does democracy mean?
2. Name three democratic practices at school.
3. Why might a secret ballot be useful?
4. Explain why the elected representative should listen to people who voted for another candidate.
5. Write four steps for conducting a fair class election.

chapters.title: Children's government in school
learning_outcomes: Describe possible roles in a children's government.
Explain the functions of learner representatives.
Take part in a supervised council activity.
Show respect while raising concerns safely.

blocks.content: What you will learn

Describe possible roles in a children's government.
Explain the functions of learner representatives.
Take part in a supervised council activity.
Show respect while raising concerns safely.

A learner has an idea for improving the school library. She shares it with her class representative, who presents the idea during a meeting of learner representatives. The teacher helps the representatives discuss it and agree on a proposal to the school administration.
The composition of children's government

A children's government is a school arrangement through which learners participate in leadership and communicate their views. Schools may organise it differently. A children's government may include a chairperson or president, a deputy, a secretary, class representatives and representatives responsible for specific areas such as learning, environment or welfare.
These are examples of roles, not a compulsory structure for every school. Ask your school about its actual arrangement.
Example roles in a learner council

Role | Possible duty
Chairperson | Coordinates meetings
Secretary | Records decisions
Class representatives | Share learners' views
Welfare representatives | Raise welfare concerns with adults
This is an example, not a compulsory school structure. Adults retain responsibility for safety and administration.
The diagram shows possible roles in a learner council. Adult school leaders remain responsible for school safety, administration and decisions requiring adult authority.
What children's government does

Learner representatives may collect suggestions, present concerns, help organise approved activities and encourage learners to care for shared resources. They should listen to all learners, communicate accurately and treat people fairly. Representatives do not have permission to punish, threaten or investigate other children.

A secretary can write a record of agreed decisions. A chairperson can invite different representatives to speak. Class representatives can report the discussion back to their classmates. Learners who hold no leadership position can still participate by sharing ideas and taking part in approved activities.
Respectful participation

Respect children's government by listening to its representatives, sharing constructive suggestions and carrying out agreed safe activities. Leaders also owe respect to those they represent. If a leader behaves unfairly, report the concern through the school's trusted adult channels.
Simulate a meeting

In a supervised group, choose an imaginary issue, such as improving a reading corner. Assign roles, hear suggestions, agree on one action and record the decision. At home, write a short example of meeting minutes.
Check your understanding
1. Name four possible roles in a children's government.
2. Explain two functions of learner representatives.
3. What is the work of a meeting secretary?
4. Give one way a learner without an elected role can participate.
5. Why should a learner representative not threaten or punish classmates?

chapters.title: Leaders in our community
learning_outcomes: Identify types of community leaders.
Explain their possible duties.
Demonstrate fairness and listening in a group task.
Explain why good leadership matters.

blocks.content: What you will learn

Identify types of community leaders.
Explain their possible duties.
Demonstrate fairness and listening in a group task.
Explain why good leadership matters.

A village plans a community clean-up. Different people contribute ideas. A community leader helps organise the discussion, while trained workers and responsible adults arrange safe waste collection. Good leadership helps people work towards a common purpose.
Different community leaders

Communities have many kinds of leaders. Religious leaders may guide people in matters of faith, encourage support for others and help bring people together. Clan leaders may help members of their communities preserve traditions and discuss matters affecting families. Village leaders may help communicate community concerns, coordinate local activities and connect residents with relevant services.

Roles differ between communities and institutions. Some leaders hold formal government positions; others are recognised through community or religious arrangements. A title alone does not make someone a good leader.
What good leaders do

Good leaders listen to others, explain decisions, act honestly, encourage cooperation and take responsibility for their actions. They consider different people's needs and do not favour someone unfairly. They seek advice from people with relevant knowledge rather than pretending to know everything.

Imagine a community choosing where to hold a meeting. A good leader asks whether the location is safe, whether people with disabilities can reach it and whether the time is suitable for participants. The leader explains the decision and invites feedback.

Leadership is not limited to adults with titles. A learner can practise good leadership by organising a group task fairly, listening to a quiet group member and taking responsibility for an agreed duty.
Interview or role-play

Ask a willing community leader, through a trusted adult, about one of their duties and one quality that helps them perform it. Alternatively, use a fictional role-play in which a group must plan a safe community activity. Show how the leader listens, includes others and explains a decision.
Check your understanding
1. Identify three kinds of community leaders.
2. Explain a duty that a village leader may perform.
3. Name four qualities of a good leader.
4. How can a group leader include a learner who rarely speaks?
5. Give an example of a decision that shows honesty and fairness.

chapters.title: How county governments work
learning_outcomes: Identify the executive and assembly of a county government.
Explain the governor's duties.
Describe the role of an MCA.
Explain how county services and public participation help communities.

blocks.content: What you will learn

Identify the executive and assembly of a county government.
Explain the governor's duties.
Describe the role of an MCA.
Explain how county services and public participation help communities.
Kenya has a national government and 47 county governments. County governments bring certain public services and decisions closer to the people in different parts of the country.
The structure of county government

A county government has a county executive and a county assembly. The county executive carries out county functions and implements county laws and plans. The county governor heads the county executive, assisted by a deputy governor and other members of the county executive committee. County officers help deliver services.

The county assembly makes laws for the county, approves relevant county plans and budgets and oversees the work of the county executive. It includes elected ward representatives, called Members of County Assembly (MCAs), and other members provided for by law.
Two main parts of county government

County executive | County assembly
Governor and deputy governor | MCAs and other members
Executive committee and administration | County lawmaking and oversight
The executive implements county functions. The assembly makes county laws and oversees the executive.
The two parts have different duties and work within Kenya's Constitution and laws.
Duties of the governor

The governor provides leadership to the county executive, helps guide county development plans, oversees implementation of county policies and services and is accountable for the county executive's work. The deputy governor assists the governor. County departments and staff carry out many daily tasks.

Examples of county functions include county health services, local markets, refuse removal and certain county roads. Not every public service is the responsibility of the county government. National and county functions are defined by law.
Roles of an MCA

An elected MCA represents people in a ward in the county assembly. MCAs take part in making county laws, considering county plans and budgets and overseeing the county executive. They can raise issues affecting residents in assembly discussions. An MCA is not the same as a governor and does not personally carry out all county services.

Ward and village administrators help coordinate county administration and community participation in their areas, in accordance with their legal duties. Residents can learn about public participation opportunities and present concerns through appropriate county channels.
Our county government chart

Draw the two main parts of a county government. Under each, write two duties. With a teacher or guardian, find the current name of your county and one county service. Discuss how residents can give feedback about that service. Do not assume a named official still holds office without checking a current official source.
Check your understanding
1. How many counties are there in Kenya?
2. Name the two main parts of a county government.
3. Explain two duties of a county governor.
4. Describe two roles of an MCA.
5. A local market needs better waste collection. Explain how county services and public feedback could help.
Chapter review

Imagine your class wants to improve the school environment. Write a short plan showing good citizenship, peaceful cooperation, respect for every child's rights, fair decision-making and responsible leadership. Explain one way an adult or county service could support the activity safely.
